To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the relative population differentiation of maternally, paternaly and biparentally inherited gene loci can be predicted from the ratio of pollen dispersal to seed dispersal, that the relative population structure of these genes can be used as a basis for inferring the pollen to seed ratio and that the relative genetic distance of these genes, relative sequence divergence of these genes and their relative phylogenetic trees can be used as an additional basis for inferring this ratio.

(i) the ratio of pollen dispersal to seed dispersal among plant populations affects the population structure of biparentally, maternally and paternally (conifer chloroplastic) inherited genes; (ii) the ratio of seed dispersal to pollen dispersal among populations affects the divergence in nucleotide sequences of genes; and (iii) the ratio of gene flow by pollen to gene flow by seed affects gene phylogeny and Nei's genetic distances between populations.

(1) population differentiation for matemally inherited genes is always higher than for biparentally and paternally genes, and (2) population differentiation for biparentally genes is always higher (or lower) than for paternally genes if pollen (seed) dispersal is higher than seed (pollen) dispersal.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (i) the effects of different patterns of gene flow on the population structure of maternally, paternaly and biparentally inherited genetic markers; (ii) the use of population genetic data on the population structure, genetic distances and sequence divergence to estimate the ratio of pollen flow to seed flow among populations; (iii) the use of phylogenies to infer gene flow among populations.
the estimation of pollen to seed ratios among populations.

the effects of contrasting gene flow patterns among subpopulations for different plant genes, and how these effects may be detected in population structure, genetic distances, sequence divergence and phylogenies.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the ratio of pollen flow to seed flow among populations can be inferred from population structure, genetic distances, sequence divergence and phylogenies of biparentally and uniparentally inherited genes.
the ratio of pollen flow to seed flow among populations is best estimated from the ratio of the population differentiation of maternally inherited to paternally inherited nuclear genes.
the relative contribution of pollen flow to gene flow is best estimated by comparing the population structure of paternally inherited and maternally (or biparentally) inherited genes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, in general, the greater the asymmetry of gene flow among populations for different genes, the greater the population differentiation and genetic distance, the greater the sequence divergence between populations, the more likely the occurrence of reticulate gene phylogenies, and the easier the estimation of pollen to seed dispersal ratio.
the relative rates of gene dispersal by pollen and seeds can be estimated using data from population structure, genetic distances, sequence divergence and phylogenetic analyses.
the ratio of pollen flow to seed flow can be estimated by comparing the level of population differentiation for matemally, paternaly and biparentally inherited plant genes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ratio of pollen flow to seed flow can be estimated from population genetic data.
population genetic theory can help in the interpretation of phylogenetic patterns.

the relative contributions of pollen and seed flow to gene flow in a plant population can be estimated by comparing the population structure of biparentally, maternally and paternally transmitted genes, and the relative contributions of these two components to the total gene flow are expected to vary among plant species.
